newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMANS FEAR FLOOD DAMAGE MAY BE BILLIONS OF MARKS.
newsitem.headline: GERMANS FEAR FLOOD DAMAGE MAY BE BILLIONS OF MARKS.

text.p: Three weeks of the worst flooding in living memory along Germany's eastern border has devastated large tracts of farmland, ruined crops and wrecked villages.
The bill has yet to be calculated.

As water levels on the swollen Oder River, which forms part of Germany's frontier with Poland, fell back steadily, local officials were due to meet on Thursday in the town of Eisenhuettenstadt to start assessing the damage.

The full extent would only become clear once flood waters drained back into the river and ground water was removed, officials said. But the total cost of relief efforts, compensation and reconstruction could run into billions.

"We should wait a while longer so that we can work with concrete figures. But certainly it will be billions of marks (dollars) worth of damage," Brandenburg's Environment Minister Matthias Platzeck told Berlin's InfoRadio.
Some fear untold environmental damage, but Matthias Freude from the regional Environment Office said it did not look as bad as initially feared.
"We are talking pollution here but not an ecological catastrophe," Freude told InfoRadio. He said that experts had tested various sites for pollution levels and found damage had been limited.
The federal agricultural ministry in Bonn said the floods had affected 30 farms with 12,000 hectares (29,000 acres) of fertile land and their businesses could fold unless they received aid.
Water levels on the Oder retreated for the fourth day, leaving behind a vast muddy trail of silt, dead fish and unidentified objects.
What was once fertile farmland has been turned into mosquito-ridden swampland that could require vast resources to be regenerated into arable land again, officials said.

Germany has, however, escaped the worst of floods that killed more than 100 people in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland last month and devastated vast swathes of land, towns, farms and villages causing billions of dollars' damage.

The worst flooding here has been in the Ziltendorf basin, south of Frankfurt an der Oder, where six villages were partially or totally submerged to the rooftops, about 7,200 hectares (18,000 acres) were engulfed and 300 residents were evacuated.
North of the city in the Oderbruch basin, which lies lower than the river and is protected by a system of dikes, a further 4,500 hectares (11,000 acres) have been soaked mainly by ground water.
The Bonn agriculture ministry said the stagnant water would remain high for the near future.
Local officials said there was no guarantee the land would be fertile once the water was drained away.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl has pledged 500 million marks ($270 million) in federal government aid to the region, calling floods there in the past weeks the "worst natural disaster ever faced by newly-unified Germany".
But regional officials say this amount may be enough to tackle immediate problems, but not in the long term.

Germany and Poland have discussed the possibility of more EU aid for a joint project to rebuild weakened flood walls along both sides of the Oder.
The EU has also been asked release 30 million marks in rescheduled autumn farm support payments as soon as possible.
